paper.title_en: Optimizer or physics? Machine-learning surrogates for collision-based preparation of multipartite entangled quantum states
paper.abstract_en: Repeated partial-SWAP collisions can prepare symmetric Dicke states, including the $W$ state, without measurement or postselection. The collision sequence uses only two global collision angles, and its fidelity is evaluated after a final layer of local phase rotations is optimized numerically, so each candidate pair requires a many-qubit simulation and a phase fit. We study when learned surrogates reduce the number of such evaluations, and what limits the best-found fidelity, for 65 Dicke targets with 11--20 qubits in noiseless simulations. At 50 evaluations per target, Gaussian-process Bayesian optimization (GP-BO) exceeds fixed Sobol and grid designs by 0.088 and 0.063 in mean best-found fidelity. Bounded Nelder--Mead reaches 0.760 against 0.762 for GP-BO, and has the higher three-seed mean on 41 of the 61 targets with a reference value; in this two-parameter problem, adaptivity matters far more than the choice between the two methods. A neural-network ensemble pretrained on 750 observations from smaller systems needs 32% fewer new evaluations per target than GP-BO at comparable fidelity, but the full neural search takes 1.6 times the wall time of GP-BO in our implementation. In a separate source-only test, the best of five neural proposals per target exceeds the best of five population-model proposals by 0.070 in mean fidelity. Exact symmetries and state diagnostics help explain why the leading adaptive methods reach similar family-mean fidelities. The collisions conserve the magnitude of the bare Dicke overlap and the total-spin weights, and for the best controls on a 12-target diagnostic panel, 79% of the infidelity is an amplitude deficit that a final phase layer cannot remove, which motivates interleaved phase control.
